Describe jujutsu changes {changes} using Conventional Commits format.

<context>
- Current working directory: `{root}`
- Jujutsu workspace root: `{root}`
- File paths in change diffs are relative to the workspace root. The vcs tools auto-detect the repo by walking up from `{root}`, so no manual path juggling is needed.
</context>

Use the **conventional-commits** skill for type/scope rules.
Use the **sem** skill to understand actual code changes vs cosmetic modifications.

<format>
`<type>(<scope>): <description>`

**Scope is required** - always include a scope in parentheses.

Examples:
- `feat(auth): add passwordless login`
- `fix(api): handle empty pagination cursor`
- `chore(deps): bump react to 18.3.0`

Type selection:
- Users see new behavior → `feat`
- Users see corrected behavior → `fix`
- Otherwise → `chore` or more specific type (`refactor`, `build`, `ci`, `test`, `docs`, `perf`, `style`)

Scope guidelines:
- Use a short noun: `api`, `auth`, `ui`, `db`, `cli`, `deps`, `docs`, `agent`, `lint`, `build`
- Use repo/module/package name when working in a monorepo
- If unsure, use a generic scope like `core`, `general`, or `misc`

Description guidelines:
- Use imperative mood: "add", "fix", "remove", "update"
- No ending punctuation
- Be specific; avoid "changes", "stuff", "update things", "refactor", "improve"
- Describe actual content, not generic categories. Name what was added/changed, not that "rules" or "principles" were added.
- Name the specific files, modules, functions, or features touched
- Name the specific behavior change: what old thing was replaced, what new thing was added
- If multiple distinct changes, list them: "add X, remove Y, rename Z"
- NEVER use vague words: "improvements", "updates", "adjustments", "enhancements", "modifications"
- NEVER say "refactor" in the description itself — the type already says refactor

Bad examples (vague, generic):
- "add behavioral guidelines and core principles"
- "add agent operating principles"
- "add behavior rules"
- "update configuration"
- "improve error handling"
- "refactor module structure"

Good examples (specific, concrete):
- "add rules for dead code removal, build verification, security, debugging, architecture, and tool usage"
- "replace emulationDir with Home Manager options for mame, melonds, mgba, pcsx2, ppsspp, xemu, retroarch"
- "remove cfg/options/config wrapper from audio, hardware, power, services, and users modules"
- "add retroarch core modules for dc, gbc, n64, saturn, snes with ES-DE system definitions"
- "consolidate retroarch config from 15 separate .cfg files into single retroarch.cfg"
</format>

<sem-guidance>
- If sem shows all changes are `~` (cosmetic) → use `style:` or `format:`
- If sem shows `∆` (modified) → describe the actual behavior change
- If sem shows `+` or `-` → describe additions/removals
- Large file counts don't always mean large changes — sem reveals the truth
</sem-guidance>

<constraints>
- **NO PARALLEL EXECUTION** — Describe each commit sequentially, one at a time. Complete all steps for one commit before starting the next. Running tool calls in parallel across commits will cause incorrect or mixed results.
- **PRESERVE COMMIT ORDER** — Describe commits in the order listed above (newer first). The first commit in the list is the newest and should be described first.
</constraints>

<workflow>
For each change ID in the list above, in the order listed (newest first), do:
1. Get git hash: `vcs-log(rev="<change-id>", format="full")` — read the `hash` column (git commit hash) from the row
   Check semantic changes: `sem diff --commit <hash-from-step-1>` (use the hash, NOT parent!)
   Check changed files and hunks: `vcs-hunk-list(rev="<change-id>")` — the hunk table lists each changed file with its content-addressed hunk IDs
   If needed for context, inspect patch: `vcs-file-diff(path="*", rev="<change-id>")` — whole-tree unified diff against the parent
   Describe: `vcs-describe(hash="<change-id>", message="<type>(<scope>): <description>")`

   **VERIFY AFTER DESCRIBE** — `vcs-describe` moves the working copy. Never use `@` to verify; always re-query by the original change ID:
   `vcs-log(rev="<change-id>", format="compact")`
   Confirm the row shows the correct change ID and your new description. If verification fails, the change ID may have been rebased — widen the scope (e.g. `vcs-log(rev="all()", format="full")`) and look for the new description in the rows.
</workflow>

<template-notes>
- In `vcs-log` rows, `hash` is the git commit hash and `change` is the jj change ID; use `format="full"` to read the git hash
- When using multiple change IDs, pass a pipe-alternation revset to the tool: `vcs-log(rev="id1 | id2", format="full")`
- After `vcs-describe`, the working copy (`@`) moves — always verify with the original change ID, not `@`
- Use `rev="<change-id>"` for ALL post-desc commands: vcs-log, vcs-hunk-list, vcs-file-diff — the change ID is stable even after rebase
</template-notes>

Split jujutsu change(s) {changes} into semantically logical commits — by file boundary (vcs-file-split) or by hunk (vcs-hunk-split), chosen by change composition.

When multiple change IDs are given, apply this workflow to each change in order (newest first), one at a time; `<change-id>` below is the change currently being processed.

<context>
- Current working directory: `{root}`
- Jujutsu workspace root: `{root}`
- File paths in change diffs are relative to the workspace root. The vcs tools auto-detect the repo by walking up from `{root}`, so no manual path juggling is needed.
</context>

<granularity>
Choose the split granularity per logical grouping based on change composition:
- **File boundary** — a grouping is a whole set of files → use `vcs-file-split` (drives `jj split`): the named files go to the FIRST/bottom commit (which takes the message), every other file moves to a new child commit.
- **Within a file** — a grouping is part of one file → use `vcs-hunk-split`: the selected hunks stay in the target commit (which takes the message), every unselected hunk moves to a new child commit.
You can mix both across iterations of the same change.
</granularity>

<workflow>
1. Get git hash: `vcs-log(rev="<change-id>", format="full")` — read the `hash` column (git commit hash) from the row
2. Check semantic changes: `sem diff --commit <hash-from-step-1>` (use the hash, NOT parent!)
3. List changed files and hunks: `vcs-hunk-list(rev="<change-id>")` — the hunk table lists each changed file with its content-addressed hunk IDs; the `files` column of `vcs-log` gives the full file list for file-boundary splits
4. Identify logical groupings by domain/purpose using sem output; choose the granularity per grouping (file boundary → `vcs-file-split`, within-file → `vcs-hunk-split`) and map each grouping to its files or hunks
5. Split iteratively:
   - File-boundary split: `vcs-file-split(rev="<change-id>", files=["<file>", ...], message="feat(scope): add feature A")` — the named files go to the FIRST/bottom commit (which takes the message); every other file moves to a new child commit (note its new change ID from the output). Re-run on the new child commit to peel off the next file group.
   - Within-file (hunk) split: `vcs-hunk-split(rev="<change-id>", hunks=["<file>=<hunk-id>", ...], message="feat(scope): add feature A")` — the target commit keeps the selected hunks and takes the message; every unselected hunk moves to a new child commit (note its new change ID from the output). Re-run `vcs-hunk-list` on the new child commit to read its remaining hunk IDs, then `vcs-hunk-split(rev="<new-child-change-id>", hunks=["<file>=<hunk-id>", ...], message="fix(scope): resolve issue B")`.
   - Each iteration keeps the selected files/hunks in the current commit and pushes the rest to a new child commit
   - Continue until all logical groupings are separated
6. Update remaining change description: `vcs-describe(hash="<change-id>", message="chore(scope): update remaining files")`
7. **VERIFY** — After each `vcs-file-split` / `vcs-hunk-split` / `vcs-describe`, verify using the original change ID (not `@`):
   `vcs-log(rev="<change-id>", format="compact")` — the `change` and description columns show the new description
</workflow>

<split-explanation>
- Choose granularity by change composition: whole-file groupings use `vcs-file-split` (named files → bottom commit, rest → new child commit); within-file groupings use `vcs-hunk-split` (selected hunks stay, unselected hunks → new child commit)
- Each split keeps the selected files/hunks in the current commit and pushes the rest to a new child commit stacked on top
- For iterative splitting, work down the chain: split the original, then split the new child commit, then its child, creating a chain:
  `original -> new1 -> new2 -> new3...`
- For hunk splits, always re-run `vcs-hunk-list` on the most recent child commit to read its remaining hunk IDs before the next split — content-addressed hunk IDs are stable, but the set of remaining hunks shrinks each step. For file splits, re-read the remaining files from `vcs-log` / `vcs-file-diff` on the child commit.
- **Important**: Split sequentially, one grouping at a time, waiting for each split to complete before starting the next. Each split rewrites the target commit, so running splits out of order or in parallel can introduce merge conflicts.
</split-explanation>

<sem-guidance>
- Use sem to identify actual behavioral changes vs cosmetic modifications
- Group files by semantic entities (functions, classes, types) that were changed
- If sem shows all changes are `~` (cosmetic), consider keeping as a single style/format commit
- Split commits by semantic boundaries, not just file boundaries
- Large file counts don't always mean large changes — sem reveals the truth
</sem-guidance>

**All commit messages MUST use Conventional Commits format: `type(scope): description`.**
- Scope is always required. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `perf`, `build`, `ci`.
- Use the **conventional-commits** skill for full rules.
- Use the **sem** skill to understand actual code changes vs cosmetic modifications.
- Descriptions MUST be specific: name the files, modules, functions, or features touched
- NEVER use vague words: "improvements", "updates", "adjustments", "enhancements", "modifications"
- NEVER say "refactor" in the description — the type already says refactor

Review the jujutsu change(s) {changes} using entity-level code analysis.

When multiple change IDs are given, apply this workflow to each change in order (newest first); `<change-id>` below is the change currently being processed.

<workflow>
1. Get git hash: `vcs-log(rev="<change-id>", format="full")` — read the `hash` column (git commit hash) from the row
2. Run code review: `code-review(target="<hash-from-step-1>")`
3. Analyze the entity-level review output (risk scores, changed entities, blast radius)
4. Address all issues found by code-review
</workflow>

<template-notes>
- Always use `rev="<change-id>"` for the vcs tools — never use `@` unless explicitly targeting the working copy
</template-notes>
